Whale
hwāl
n. (a great sea creature; the Authorized Version's rendering for the largest inhabitants of the deep)
Old English hwael, a large sea-beast. The Authorized Version uses it for Hebrew tannin (a great sea creature or monster) and for Greek ketos (a huge fish or sea-beast) — in neither case a term of modern zoological classification.

Biblical Definition

The word enters Scripture on the fifth day: “And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind” (Genesis 1:21). It is the first appearance of the verb create since verse one, which is a mark of how the text regards these creatures — not as chaos-monsters wrestled into submission, as the surrounding nations told it, but as made, and pronounced good. Job asks, “Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?” (Job 7:12), and Ezekiel uses the figure for Pharaoh thrashing in his rivers (Ezekiel 32:2). But the weight of the word rests on our Lord's use of it: “For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). Jonah records that “the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah” (Jonah 1:17). Christ takes that history as history and makes it the one sign granted to a generation demanding proof — the sign of the prophet Jonas, which is burial and resurrection.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the whale as the largest of marine animals, of the order Cete, and notes the scriptural use for great fishes of the sea.

expand to see more

WHALE, n. The general name of an order of animals inhabiting the ocean, arranged in zoology under the name of Cete or Cetacea.

2. In scripture, a name given to great fishes or sea-monsters generally.

MONSTER, n. An animal of a form different from that which nature usually produces.

DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean.

SIGN, n. That by which anything is shown, made known or represented; a token; a wonder.

Key Scripture

Matthew 12:40 — "For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth."

Genesis 1:21 — "And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good."

Jonah 1:17 — "Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights."

Job 7:12 — "Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?"

Modern Corruption

The great fish is made the test case for treating Old Testament narrative as legend, and the Lord who cited it as history is quietly overruled.

expand to see more

Jonah has long been the standard exhibit for the claim that the historical books contain legendary material — a moral fable about a reluctant prophet, not a record of events. The difficulty for that reading is not zoological but doctrinal. Christ founded an argument about His own burial and resurrection on the case, offered it as the only sign His generation would receive, and in the following verse spoke of the men of Nineveh rising in the judgment because they repented at Jonah's preaching. A sign drawn from a story that did not happen is no sign, and men who did not exist do not rise in the judgment. To make Jonah a fable is to correct the Lord Jesus on a matter of fact He treated as decisive.

A second and lesser confusion arises from pressing the English word into modern taxonomy and then declaring an error, since ketos and Hebrew tannin denote a great sea-creature without specifying an order of mammals. The Authorized Version is not making a claim about cetaceans. Jonah 1:17 says the LORD prepared a great fish, which locates the event where the text locates it — in the providence of God, not in the ordinary habits of marine life. The miracle was never that a fish was large. It was that God appointed it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tannin, a great sea creature — Genesis 1:21, Ezekiel 32:2, Job 7:12; Greek ketos (G2785), a sea-monster — Matthew 12:40, its only occurrence.

expand to see more

Hebrew tannin — sea creature, monster, serpent; Genesis 1:21 where God creates them, and Ezekiel 32:2 of Pharaoh.

Greek ketos (G2785) — a huge fish or sea-beast; Matthew 12:40 only.

Hebrew dag gadol — a great fish; Jonah 1:17, prepared by the LORD.

Genesis 1:21 uses bara, to create, for the first time since Genesis 1:1 — these creatures are made, not subdued.

Matthew 12:39-41 makes the episode the sign of the prophet Jonas and appeals to the Ninevites as real men who repented.

Usage

"“Three days and three nights in the whale's belly” — the one sign given to an evil generation."

"“God created great whales” — made and called good, not chaos to be conquered."

"The LORD prepared the fish; the appointing is the miracle."
